findings.text: Global quality of service state aggregates a prioritized holder list with three signed 32 bit slots for current target, built in default and unconstrained value, plus a selector choosing largest versus smallest aggregation and a pointer to blocking change notifiers.

Request state for global constraints pairs a priority list element with a back pointer to its aggregate. Flag requests pair a doubly linked element with a signed 32 bit mask. Flag aggregate pairs a list head with one effective signed 32 bit mask.

Frequency domain keeps separate minimum and maximum aggregates each with its own notifier chain. A frequency request records whether it targets minimum or maximum, holds a priority element and points at its domain. Device request records a request category, a variant payload for priority or flags or frequency, and its device. Device aggregate holds resume and tolerance aggregates, a frequency domain, a flag aggregate and three saved pointers for default resume, tolerance and flag requests.

Flag coverage reports four ordered outcomes from undefined at negative one through none, some and all. Generic default is negative one. Unrestricted latency uses largest signed 32 bit value, with a nanosecond form scaled by one thousand. CPU latency default is two thousand seconds in microseconds. Resume default and no constraint equal unrestricted latency. Tolerance default is zero and its no constraint is negative one. Minimum frequency default is zero and maximum frequency default equals the frequency maximum default. The no power off flag is the lowest bit.

Aggregation selector orders uninitialized first, then largest, then smallest. Frequency constraints default minimum to zero and maximum to largest signed 32 bit value. Frequency request categories number minimum as one and maximum next. Device categories number resume latency one, tolerance two, minimum frequency three, maximum frequency four and flags five. Request lifecycle orders add first, update second and remove third.

Runtime control flags use five distinct single bits with values one, two, four, eight and sixteen. In order they mean asynchronous handling, no waiting for a concurrent transition, combined usage count get and put accounting, use of autosuspend delay, and transparent success while runtime management is disabled.
A device quality request counts as active exactly when its device pointer is present. A frequency request counts as active exactly when its domain pointer is present and not an error marker.

Disabled CPU latency helpers report a fixed large limit, report requests as inactive, and accept add, update and remove as silent no operations. CPU wakeup limit helper reports the unrestricted resume value.

Disabled device quality helpers return undefined flag coverage, unrestricted resume latency, frequency defaults or zero, and success for add, update, remove, notifier, ancestor, expose and tolerance operations. Initialization marks device power state as on and destruction marks it invalid. Hide and flag update helpers have no effect.

Enabled accessors for requested resume latency and requested flags follow stored request pointers without visible checks, so callers must ensure quality state and the corresponding saved request exist. The raw resume accessor tolerates absent quality state by returning the unrestricted value. Disabled fallbacks always report success or defaults and can mask absent support.

Wakeup accounting holds a name, numeric identifier, list linkage, wake interrupt association, timer with expiry, several monotonic duration accumulators and last event stamps, five unsigned counters for events, activations, relaxations, expiries and wakeups, an owning device pointer, and two single bit states for active and autosleep enable. A walk helper iterates all sources from start to next.
Wakeup accounting embeds a spin lock alongside its list, timer, counters and timing fields, indicating that concurrent updates to wakeup state are serialized by that lock.

Suspended means runtime status suspended while enable depth is zero. Active means status active or enable depth nonzero. Status suspended checks status alone. Enabled means enable depth zero. Blocked reflects a recorded blocked last status. Callback absence and interrupt safe mode each mirror a dedicated device power flag.

Reference acquisition without resume increments the device usage count. Release without idle decrements only when nonzero. Marking busy records a fast monotonic timestamp. Child ignore control stores a boolean in device power state.

Public runtime transitions are thin wrappers over idle, suspend and resume primitives with flag combinations. Synchronous forms pass no flags. Asynchronous request forms add async. Get forms add get-put accounting, with active acquisition undoing the count on failure. Autosuspend forms refresh the busy stamp and add the autosuspend flag. Put forms use idle except for suspend and autosuspend variants that use suspend. Status helpers force active or suspended. Disable, autosuspend enable and autosuspend disable forward a boolean to internal setters.

When runtime management is unavailable, queueing reports failure, idle and suspend report not supported, resume reports already resumed, schedule and conditional get report invalid, generic and force suspend succeed while force resume reports no such device, need not resume is always true, suspended and enabled report false, active and blocked report true, and barrier, enable, allow, autosuspend, supplier and link helpers are silent no operations.

Runtime surface includes work queueing on a dedicated queue, generic suspend and resume, forced suspend and resume, conditional acquisition, barrier, block and unblock while disabled, enable, allow and forbid, managed enable and acquisition, autosuspend delay and expiry, no I O allocation mode, supplier reference and link management, scoped acquisition helpers for active with autosuspend and enabled variants plus an error accessor, and macros defining and exporting runtime operation tables from suspend, resume and idle callbacks.
